transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-23 16:21 UTC
Duration: 56 min
Attendees: Ava Chen, Diego Martinez, Liam O'Rourke (Redwood); Elena Park, Marcus Flynn, Priya Nair, Samir Patel (Monarch)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Quick discovery on cost levers for inference. Customer has low-latency checkout use case, wants guidance on per-token cost and options for Dedicated vs Hosted given budget constraints.

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick round of intros, then we want to make sure we understand your workload — latency targets, volume, and any security constraints. Elena, do you want to kick off?
[00:18] Elena: Yeah sure, hi all. I'm Elena, Head of AI at Monarch. We're rolling personalization into checkout — recommendations, short-form copy tweaks, and fraud checks in the pipeline. Latency is... like, 150 to 200ms tail at the 95th percentile is kind of our bar for the checkout path. CPU-based infra can't meet that for the generation bits so we're evaluating inference providers. Main ask today is to understand per-token unit costs and what levers we have to tune cost while preserving latency.
[00:42] Ava: Absolutely. Diego and Liam from engineering will run through batching, caching, and deployment options. Marcus — can you share rough qps or token volumes?
[00:52] Marcus: Sure, today we have 700k unique sessions a day, about 15% hit the personalized flow — so roughly 100k requests a day initially. Each request averages 120 tokens output and maybe 40 tokens input => call it 160 tokens. Peak qps during sales spikes might be 40 rps. Budget wise, upper bound for pilot is about $8k/month for inference.
[01:20] Diego: Got it. Couple of framing points: per-token price varies by model and deployment. Hosted gives simplest per-token billing and we can show exact cost at different batch sizes. Dedicated is a reserved GPU pool — you pay for capacity but get much lower per-token compute cost at scale, plus isolation. Private adds operational overhead but is required for strict control over keys and network.
[01:44] Samir: Priya will have questions about keys and logs, so maybe hold space for that.
[01:49] Priya: Yeah, two things up front: we need KMS integration (HSM optional), audit logs forwarded to our SIEM, and SSO for console access. Data residency is EU-only for a subset of PII.
[02:05] Ava: That's helpful. We support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated, and hosted can integrate with our partner KMS for enterprise plans. Audit logs and RBAC are standard on Dedicated/Private — we'll share the checklist.
[02:18] Elena: Cool. On cost, what's the baseline per-token on Hosted for a 13B-ish model? Ballpark.
[02:24] Diego: Ballpark you might see $0.0007 to $0.002 per token on Hosted depending on model and SLO. That's end-to-end including Redwood infra margin. But the key is batching and prefix caching: if most of your requests share prefixes (e.g., same system prompt + common product metadata), caching K/V across requests can reduce repeated generation work dramatically. That changes effective tokens computed, not tokens billed by some providers — Redwood will bill on output tokens but our batching + cache reductions lower compute and thus cost tiers in Dedicated.
[02:56] Marcus: Can you explain how caching works with short personalization? Our prompts vary per user but product catalog pieces are the same.
[03:04] Diego: Sure. Two common levers: prefix caching — we cache the model KV state for the shared prefix (system prompt + product catalog/context). Then for each request we only compute the user-specific suffix. That makes each request effectively shorter in compute. Second is response caching — if you get identical outputs for identical inputs, we can return from cache.
[03:24] Elena: So if shared prefix is like 80 tokens, and dynamic is 40, we only recompute 40 tokens per request?
[03:30] Diego: Exactly in ideal cases. There are caveats with sampling and temperature changes; but for deterministic generation or constrained sampling it's quite effective.
[03:38] Liam: Also batching across simultaneous requests reduces per-token kernel overhead. Continuous batching latency is tuned so small batches don't blow up tail latency — important for your 150-200ms SLO.
[03:48] Priya: How predictable is Dedicated autoscaling? We need capacity guarantees, SLOs.
[03:53] Ava: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed capacity targets and configurable autoscale/burst policies. You reserve a baseline GPU pool for steady-state then allow controlled burst to shared capacity. For Monarch's pilot volumes, a small Dedicated pool could be cost-effective if you hit higher qps.
[04:08] Marcus: Walk me through an example: given our 100k requests/day at 160 tokens avg, and with prefix caching reducing compute to 40 tokens per request on average, what costs look like Hosted vs Dedicated.
[04:19] Diego: Quick back-of-envelope — 100k * 40 = 4M compute tokens/day. On Hosted at $0.0012/token compute-equivalent that's $4,800/day? Wait that would be too high, typo — let me recalc. If it's $0.0008 per token then 4M * $0.0008 = $3,200 per day, which is wrong scale. Sorry mixing units - that's per thousand?
[04:44] Speaker 1: (overlap) I think the model prices are per thousand tokens often, like $0.8 per k?
[04:50] Diego: Right — sorry for confusion. Redwood bills per 1k tokens in to be comparable — example: $0.80 per 1k output tokens for a particular 13B endpoint on Hosted. So take 4M tokens/day => 4,000 * $0.80 = $3,200/day, which monthly would blow past your pilot. But with prefix caching reducing the billed output tokens and batching plus quantization you can bring that down. If your effective billed tokens are 600k/day then at $0.80 per 1k it's $480/day.
[05:19] Elena: The math is what we need — it's easy to blow the budget.
[05:23] Ava: Totally. That's why we sent sample worksheets in similar pilots — show per-1k token rates, sample batch sizes, cache hit rates, and how Dedicated changes the compute unit cost because you amortize the GPU fixed cost. For Dedicated, you'd model monthly reserved GPU cost + very low per-token incremental cost if you fully utilize.
[05:41] Marcus: What's quantization's impact? We run a 13B model — can lower precision help cost and latency?
[05:46] Diego: Yes. INT8/4-bit quantization reduces memory footprint and can allow higher batching density or lower-cost GPUs. That typically lowers per-token cost but may introduce small quality regressions. Redwood Optimize recommends quant profiles per workload; we can run evals on your prompts to test quality vs latency tradeoffs.
[06:04] Samir: Are we able to test with our exact prompts in a pilot?
[06:07] Diego: Absolutely — pilot harness runs your prompt set and measures latency, tokens, and quality metrics. We'll need about a 2–3 hour tokenized run with representative traffic shape.
[06:16] Priya: On security, you mentioned audit logs and KMS. What about network topology for Private — we need to know if any egress to Redwood control plane hits our VPC.
[06:25] Ava: For Private deployments you can run both control plane and data plane in your VPC; or control plane hosted with private peering. We'll share a network diagram. We also support customer-managed KMS and key rotations.
[06:36] Priya: Good. Also need pen-test and compliance evidence.
[06:39] Ava: We'll include SOC 2 and the pen test summary in the package.
[06:44] Elena: Back to cost levers — you mentioned routing policies?
[06:47] Liam: Yes: smart routing lets you route low-latency critical traffic to higher-tier nodes or smaller models, and lower-priority batch requests to cheaper nodes or quantized variants. You can also implement fallback policies — e.g., if Dedicated capacity is saturated, fall back to hosted cheaper model or return cached response. That protects availability and cost.
[07:06] Marcus: How do you measure effective token reductions from caching in practice?
[07:10] Diego: We instrument per-request compute tokens vs billed tokens. In Dedicated, you get token-level traces and KV cache hit metrics. For Hosted we can provide aggregated estimates. We'll run an initial profiling to estimate cache hit rate; in similar retail pilots we saw 40–60% compute reduction from prefix caching.
[07:28] Elena: That's promising. What's the lift to implement prefix caching on our side?
[07:32] Liam: Minimal: you identify the stable context (catalog, system prompt) and call our SDK to materialize caches. There's also an option to let Redwood infer prefixes automatically but explicit caching gives best results.
[07:44] Priya: Any PCI considerations for checkout-related PII?
[07:47] Ava: We recommend tokenizing/excluding direct card data; Redwood can run in Private mode if you need to keep PII inside your VPC. We also support field-level redaction in transit.
[07:58] Elena: Ok, timeline — we want to pilot in Q2, ideally start by early April. What do you need from us to get a pilot scoped?
[08:06] Diego: For pilot: sample prompt set and traffic shape, expected latency SLO, desired success criteria (cost target + latency target + quality thresholds), and security constraints. From Redwood we'll send a pilot plan, pricing worksheet, and a small dedicated cluster proposal if needed.
[08:21] Marcus: Can you put numbers on the small dedicated cluster? Like cost to reserve a 1–2 GPU pool for a month?
[08:26] Liam: Rough numbers: a small Dedicated baseline (2x A10G-style GPUs equivalent) could be $6k–$12k/month depending on region and support tier. When you amortize across tokens the per-token compute drops significantly compared to Hosted. We'll put exact quotes in the worksheet.
[08:45] Speaker 2: (murmur)
[08:47] Diego: Also note caching plus batching plus quantization is multiplicative: caching reduces compute tokens, quantization reduces cost per token, batching reduces per-token kernel overhead. The pilot will measure where your workload lands on that curve.
[08:59] Priya: For the pilot run — will Redwood sign an NDA and data handling addendum?
[09:03] Ava: Yes, we have a standard NDA and DPA. We'll push those to legal once we have the contact.
[09:09] Elena: Any hard limits on throughput for hosted? If we go hosted for pilot and then convert to Dedicated, what's the migration complexity?
[09:18] Liam: Hosted scales well but it's a shared pool; there are soft rate limits at default - we can bump them for pilots. Migration is straightforward: same API surface, just switch model endpoints and pin to Dedicated; we support canary deploys and routing.
[09:31] Marcus: Regarding observability — we need token-level cost breakdown per route, and traces for tail latency causes.
[09:38] Diego: Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdown, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. You can also pull raw logs to your observability stack.
[09:46] Samir: One practical question — how do you handle retries and idempotency when caching is involved?
[09:51] Diego: We provide idempotency tokens and careful TTLs on cache entries to avoid serving stale outputs. For deterministic outputs you can cache aggressively; for sampling-heavy flows we recommend shorter TTLs.
[10:03] Elena: This has been helpful. A few clarifying questions on numbers: can you send a worked example comparing Hosted per-1k rates with a Dedicated amortized example for our 100k requests/day and target $8k/month?
[10:15] Ava: Yes — that's the pricing worksheet item. We'll show Hosted line items, a Dedicated reserve scenario, and a sensitivity table over cache hit rates (0%, 30%, 60%).
[10:26] Priya: Also need to see the network diagram and KMS integration options before legal signs anything.
[10:31] Ava: We'll include that.
[10:34] Elena: Any immediate red flags?
[10:36] Diego: Nothing major. The risk is if effective billed tokens remain high and you stay on Hosted, the monthly cost could overshoot your pilot budget. The pilot mitigates that by proving cache-hit rates and allowing dedicated sizing.
[10:48] Marcus: Ok let's close with next steps and owners.
[10:51] Ava: Recap — Redwood will: 1) Send pricing worksheet and sensitivity tables (Ava), 2) Draft pilot benchmark plan and required harness (Diego), 3) Send SOC2/pen-test summary and Private deployment checklist/network diagram (Liam). Monarch will: 1) Share sample prompts & traffic shape (Elena/Marcus), 2) Share security constraints and KMS requirements (Priya).
[11:15] Elena: Good. We'll aim to get docs to you by 2027-02-26.
[11:20] Ava: Great, we'll target the pilot plan by 2027-02-28. Any final quick questions?
[11:25] Priya: Nothing else from security.
[11:27] Samir: Nope. Thanks everyone.
[11:29] Ava: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the pack.

(Transcript end — system note: occasional transcription errors present, e.g., K V cache transcribed as KV cash in spots.)
